docs.title: 15.1 — Reinsurance Introduction & History
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define reinsurance and explain its purpose.
  2. Describe the key functions reinsurance serves for a primary insurer.
  3. Explain the evolution of the reinsurance market.
  4. Identify the principal participants in the reinsurance market.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. A primary (direct) insurer cedes part of its risk to a reinsurer in exchange for a premium, protecting its balance sheet against individual large losses and accumulations. Reinsurance supports capacity, stabilises loss experience, improves solvency, and enables insurers to write risks they could not otherwise retain. This chapter introduces the concepts, market participants, and historical development of reinsurance.

docs.title: 15.1.1 What Is Reinsurance?
docs.text:
Reinsurance is a contract under which one insurer (the ceding company or cedent) transfers all or part of a risk or portfolio of risks to another insurer (the reinsurer) in exchange for a premium.

Term Definition Ceding company / cedent The primary insurer that transfers risk Reinsurer The insurer that assumes the transferred risk Cession The amount of risk transferred to the reinsurer Retention / net line The amount of risk the ceding company keeps Retrocession Reinsurance of a reinsurer's liabilities Retrocessionaire The reinsurer that accepts retrocession

docs.title: Purpose of Reinsurance
docs.text: Function Description Capacity Enable writing larger individual risks than net resources allow Catastrophe protection Protect against accumulations of loss (windstorm, earthquake, flood) Stabilisation Smooth loss experience between good and bad years Solvency Reduce required capital and improve solvency ratios Capital management Release capital for growth or return to shareholders Expertise Access market knowledge, pricing, and risk engineering Portfolio management Manage exposure concentration by line, class, or territory New venture support Support entry into new markets and products

docs.title: Proportional Flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Policyholder] -->|Premium| B[Primary Insurer]
    B -->|Ceded premium| C[Reinsurer]
    C -->|Share of losses| B
    B -->|Claims payment| A

docs.title: Contract Relationship
docs.text: Element Primary Contract Reinsurance Contract Parties Policyholder & insurer Ceding company & reinsurer Subject Risk (property/person) Liabilities of the ceding company Premium Policy premium Ceded premium / reinsurance premium Duration Policy term Treaty term (often 12 months) Applicable law Policy contract Reinsurance contract Claim Policyholder claim Recovery from reinsurer

docs.title: 15.1.3 Key Market Participants
docs.text: Participant Role Primary insurers Write direct risks; purchase reinsurance Professional reinsurers Dedicated reinsurance companies (e.g., Munich Re, Swiss Re) Reinsurance brokers Intermediaries who place reinsurance (e.g., Guy Carpenter, Aon Re, Gallagher Re) Lloyd's of London Market where syndicates underwrite reinsurance Specialist carriers Insurance groups with reinsurance divisions Retrocessionaires Accept risk from other reinsurers Capital market participants ILS, catastrophe bonds, industry loss warranties Regulators Supervise solvency and reinsurance transactions Rating agencies Assess reinsurer security and claims-paying ability

docs.title: Reinsurer Security
docs.text: Consideration Why It Matters Credit rating A.M. Best, S&P, Moody's, Fitch ratings of the reinsurer Collateral Trust funds for alien reinsurers writing in the US Cedent credit risk Reinsurer may fail to pay recoveries Regulatory recognition State/territory approval of credit for reinsurance

docs.title: 15.1.4 History of Reinsurance
docs.text: Era Development 14th century Marine insurance emerges in Italian city-states c. 1347 Earliest insurance contracts issued; reinsurance-like agreements appear 17th century Lloyd's Coffee House (1688) — Lloyd's of London develops 1800s Modern reinsurance companies form: Kölnische Rück (1846), Swiss Re (1863), Munich Re (1880) 1906 San Francisco earthquake — major test of reinsurance market 1900s Treaty reinsurance evolves; proportional structures dominate 1950s–1970s Excess of loss treaties increase in popularity 1980s Financial reinsurance and alternative structures emerge 1990s Catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities (ILS) develop 2000s–2010s Convergence of capital markets and reinsurance; sidecars, ILWs 2020s Data analytics, AI-driven underwriting, cyber reinsurance growth

docs.title: 1906 San Francisco Earthquake
docs.text: Example: The 1906 earthquake and subsequent fire caused insured losses representing a significant fraction of US insurers' capital at the time. Several insurers defaulted, demonstrating the importance of reinsurance capacity and leading to more structured catastrophe protection.

docs.title: For Individual Risks
docs.text: Benefit Example Larger limits A $100M airline risk with $20M net capacity requires $80M reinsurance Specialised perils Nuclear, aviation, satellite Facultative placement Single large risk placed case by case

docs.title: For Catastrophes
docs.text: Element Description Catastrophe XL Excess of loss inure to a single event Aggregation Protection across a portfolio Non-proportional Reinsurer pays above an attachment point Modelling Cat models assess probable maximum loss (PML)

docs.title: For Solvency & Capital
docs.text: Element Description Risk-based capital Reinsurance reduces required capital Solvency II / regulatory capital Credit for reinsurance under solvency frameworks Earnings stability Protect against volatile experience Recovery of losses Reinsurer pays its share of claims

docs.title: 15.1.6 Insurance vs Reinsurance
docs.text: Aspect Insurance Reinsurance Contracting parties Policyholder and insurer Insurer and reinsurer Subject matter Original risk Insurer's liability on original risk Insurable interest Policyholder's interest Cedent's exposure Regulation Extensive consumer protection Wholesale, less consumer protection Claimant Policyholder Ceding company Distribution Agents, brokers, direct Reinsurance brokers, direct

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Cession Risk transferred to a reinsurer Ceding company Insurer transferring risk Retention Risk kept by the ceding company Retrocession Reinsurance of reinsurer liabilities Reinsurer Insurer assuming transferred risk

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Reinsurance is insurance for insurers — it transfers risk from a primary insurer to a reinsurer.
  2. It serves capacity, catastrophe protection, stabilisation, and capital functions.
  3. The market includes professional reinsurers, brokers, Lloyd's, and capital markets.
  4. Historical catastrophes shaped modern reinsurance structures.

docs.title: 15.2 — Facultative Reinsurance
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define facultative reinsurance and explain when it is used.
  2. Describe the facultative placement process.
  3. Distinguish facultative from treaty reinsurance.
  4. Identify the advantages, disadvantages, and underwriting considerations.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Facultative reinsurance is purchased for an individual risk on a case-by-case basis. Each facultative session is separately underwritten, priced, and documented. It is used to provide capacity above treaty limits, cover specialised risks, and manage unusual exposures that fall outside an automatic treaty.

docs.title: 15.2.1 What Is Facultative Reinsurance?
docs.text:
Facultative reinsurance is a single-risk reinsurance arrangement under which the reinsurer has the "faculty" (option) to accept or decline each individual risk submitted. The ceding company likewise has no obligation to cede.

Feature Description Object Individual risk / single policy Submission Case by case Underwriting Full individual risk assessment Documentation Facultative certificate / slip Premium Negotiated per risk Duration Policy period of the underlying risk

docs.title: 15.2.2 When Is Facultative Used?
docs.text: Scenario Example Capacity above treaty Policy limit exceeds automatic treaty capacity Specialised risks Satellite, aviation hull, large industrial works New / unusual risks Emerging risks with no rating history Adverse experience Poor loss history requiring individual scrutiny Portfolio shaping Exclude specific risks from a treaty Pre-reinsurance Secure cover before entering a binding treaty Non-treaty classes Risks not covered by existing treaties

docs.title: Facultative vs Treaty
docs.text: Aspect Facultative Treaty Coverage Individual risk Portfolio / class of business Underwriting Each risk separately Program level Obligation Optional both sides Automatic within terms Documentation Certificate per risk One treaty agreement Administration Per-risk documentation Program level reporting Cost Higher per-risk expense Lower expense per risk Speed Slower — negotiation Faster — automatic Certainty Not guaranteed Guaranteed within scope

docs.title: 15.2.3 The Facultative Placement Process
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Cedent identifies risk] --> B[Prepare submission pack]
    B --> C[Submit to reinsurer / broker]
    C --> D{Reinsurer reviews}
    D -->|Accept| E[Negotiate terms]
    D -->|Decline| F[Return to cedent]
    E --> G[Issue certificate]
    G --> H[Premium payment]
    H --> I[Risk in force]

docs.title: Submission Pack Contents
docs.text: Document Purpose Completed risk proposal Key risk facts Underlying policy wording Coverage to be reinsured Loss history Past claims experience Financial information Insured's stability Survey / inspection report Physical risk condition Photos / maps Site information Valuation evidence Sum insured basis Treaty details Existing coverage and exclusions

docs.title: Slip / Certificate Key Fields
docs.text: Field Description Reinsured name Ceding company Original insured Underlying policyholder Period Underlying policy period Interest Risk / subject matter Situation Location of risk Valuation Sum insured and basis Limits Reinsurer's share and limits Premium Rate and amount Conditions Facultative conditions and follow-the-fortunes wording

docs.title: Key Underwriting Factors
docs.text: Factor Assessment PML / MFL Probable maximum loss / maximum foreseeable loss Sum insured Adequate and not inflated Construction & occupancy Property risk characteristics Protection Sprinklers, alarms, security Exposure Natural perils, accumulation, third-party Loss history Frequency, severity, trends Management Risk attitude and loss control Basis of valuation Reinstatement vs indemnity

docs.title: Risk Accumulation Control
docs.text: Element Description Same risk Multiple interests in one location Catastrophe accumulation Exposure to one event across the book Common causation Same origin (fire, flood) affecting many policies Geocoding Map exposures for cat accumulation

docs.title: 15.2.5 Facultative Pricing
docs.text: Component Description Rate on line (ROL) Premium as % of limit Exposure basis Rate per $100 of sum insured Experience basis Trended loss history Expense loading Brokerage, commission, administration Cost of capital Return required on the risk Profit / contingency Risk margin

docs.title: Simple Pricing Illustration
docs.text: Element Value Sum insured $50,000,000 Net retention $10,000,000 Facultative limit $40,000,000 Rate 0.20% of sum insured Premium $100,000 Rate on line 0.25% of limit

docs.title: Advantages for the Cedent
docs.text: Advantage Description Capacity Enhance ability to write large risks Flexibility Tailor cover to each risk Protection Reduce net exposure on specific large risks Competition Access multiple reinsurance markets Knowledge Reinsurer risk engineering input

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text: Disadvantage Description Cost Higher administrative cost per risk Delay Time to secure cover Uncertainty Cover may not be available / renewed Management burden Per-risk negotiation and documentation

docs.title: 15.2.7 Example — Facultative Placement
docs.text:
Example — Large Industrial Property:

  • Risk: Chemical plant, $120M sum insured.
  • Cedent retention: $20M.
  • Existing treaty capacity: $50M.
  • Facultative placed: $50M excess of $70M.

Analysis: The cedent retains $20M, uses $50M treaty, and places a $50M facultative layer to reach the full $120M. The facultative reinsurer underwrites the plant's protection, occupancy, and management before agreeing.

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. Define facultative reinsurance.
  2. List five situations where facultative reinsurance is used.
  3. Describe the key sections of a facultative slip.
  4. What is rate on line and why does it matter?
  5. Compare the costs of facultative vs treaty reinsurance.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Facultative Optional, case-by-case reinsurance Slip Document summarising facultative terms Rate on line Premium as % of limit Follow the fortunes Reinsurer follows cedent's claims decisions

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Facultative is individual-risk reinsurance with full underwriting on each risk.
  2. It provides capacity and covers risks outside treaty scope.
  3. Placement involves submission, negotiation, and certification.
  4. Cost is higher and processing slower than treaty.

docs.title: 15.3 — Treaty Reinsurance: Quota Share & Surplus
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define treaty reinsurance and its key features.
  2. Explain quota share and surplus reinsurance structures.
  3. Calculate cessions, retentions, and recoveries for proportional treaties.
  4. Describe commutations, reports, and administration of proportional treaties.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Treaty reinsurance covers a defined portfolio or class of business automatically within agreed terms. In a quota share treaty the ceding company and reinsurer share every risk in a fixed ratio. In a surplus treaty the reinsurer provides capacity above the cedent's retention, sharing the surplus line on a proportional basis. Both are proportional structures — premium and losses are shared in the same proportion as the risk.

docs.title: 15.3.1 Treaty Reinsurance Fundamentals
docs.text:
Treaty reinsurance is an agreement under which the reinsurer automatically accepts a defined share of all risks written by the ceding company falling within the treaty's scope, without individual risk submission.

Feature Description Scope Defined class / portfolio / territory Obligation Automatic — cedent must cede, reinsurer must accept Term Usually 12 months, renewable Documentation One treaty agreement Premium Ceded premium based on underlying business Claims Reinsurer pays its share per treaty terms

docs.title: Types of Treaty
docs.text: Type Category Structure Quota share (QS) Proportional Fixed % of every risk Surplus Proportional Capacity above retention, variable share Excess of loss (XL) Non-proportional Losses above attachment Stop loss Non-proportional Aggregate loss ratio protection Catastrophe XL Non-proportional Single event protection

docs.title: 15.3.2 Quota Share (QS) Treaty
docs.text:
Quota share reinsurance cedes a fixed percentage of every risk in the treaty portfolio to the reinsurer.

Element Description Cession Fixed % (e.g., 50%) of every risk Retention Remaining % retained by cedent Premium Same % of premium ceded Losses Same % of losses recovered Purpose Capital relief, portfolio sharing, profit sharing Commission Ceding commission often paid to cedent

docs.title: Premium & Loss Sharing
docs.text: Item Total Cedent 60% Reinsurer 40% Premium $100,000 $60,000 $40,000 Loss $50,000 $30,000 $20,000 Commission — Received Pays commission

docs.title: Ceding Commission
docs.text: Element Description Purpose Reimburse cedent's acquisition and administration costs Calculation % of ceded premium Typical range 20–35% depending on business Profit commission Additional share of reinsurer profit

docs.title: 15.3.3 Surplus Treaty
docs.text:
Surplus (surplus share) reinsurance provides proportional coverage on individual risks above the ceding company's retention up to a defined number of lines.

Concept Definition Retention / net line Amount the cedent retains per risk Line Unit of retention (e.g., $500,000) Surplus capacity Number of lines (e.g., 10 lines = 10 × retention) Cession The surplus above retention ceded to reinsurer Automatic facility Cover provided automatically within capacity

docs.title: Surplus Treaty Illustration
docs.text: Item Risk A Risk B Sum insured $500,000 $3,000,000 Retention (1 line) $500,000 $500,000 Ceded to surplus $0 $2,500,000 Lines used 0 5 Cedent % 100% 16.7% Reinsurer % 0% 83.3%

docs.title: 15.3.4 Quota Share vs Surplus Comparison
docs.text: Aspect Quota Share Surplus Share of risk Fixed % always Variable, above retention Small risks Ceded automatically Fully retained (below retention) Large risks Ceded at same % Ceded above retention Purpose Capital relief, portfolio sharing Capacity, retention protection Administration Simple — fixed % More complex — per-risk share Adverse selection Limited Large risks ceded may be riskier

docs.title: Key Calculation Formulas
docs.text: Formula Expression Cession % (surplus) (Sum insured − Retention) ÷ Sum insured Retention % Retention ÷ Sum insured Reinsurer share of loss Loss × Cession % Lines used Cession ÷ Retention

docs.title: Bordereau
docs.text: Content Description Premium bordereau List of ceded risks with premiums Loss bordereau List of claims with recoveries Frequency Monthly or quarterly Basis Underlying policy data

docs.title: Accounting
docs.text: Item Description Ceded premium Premium transferred to reinsurer Ceding commission Reinsurer pays cedent % of premium Profit commission Share of reinsurer's profit Recoveries Reinsurer's share of paid losses Reserves Funds withheld for outstanding claims Deposit premium Minimum premium at inception

docs.title: 15.3.6 Underwriting Considerations for Proportional Treaties
docs.text: Factor Assessment Retention adequacy Cedent retains meaningful risk Portfolio quality Mix of classes, territories, durations Ceding commission Appropriate for acquisition cost Claims management Cedent handles claims; follow-the-fortunes Reserving Adequate reserves for outstanding Accumulation Catastrophe exposure within proportional book Compliance Regulatory credit for reinsurance

docs.title: 15.3.7 Worked Example — Surplus Treaty
docs.text:
Example:

  • Retention: $1,000,000 (1 line)
  • Surplus capacity: 9 lines → $9,000,000
  • Risk: $5,000,000 sum insured

Calculation:

  • Cession = $5,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $4,000,000
  • Lines used = 4
  • Cession % = 80%
  • Cedent share = 20%; loss of $500,000 → cedent pays $100,000, reinsurer pays $400,000

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between quota share and surplus reinsurance?
  2. How is the surplus cession percentage calculated?
  3. What is a bordereau and what does it contain?
  4. Why does the ceding commission matter in a proportional treaty?
  5. What is the risk of adverse selection in a surplus treaty?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Bordereau Periodic schedule of risks/claims Ceding commission Reinsurer payment to cedent Lines Multiples of retention capacity Profit commission Profit share to cedent Reinstatement Restoration of cover after loss

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Quota share shares all risks in a fixed ratio.
  2. Surplus treaties share the amount above a retention, up to capacity.
  3. Premium, losses, and commissions follow the ceded share.
  4. Proportional treaties require disciplined reporting (bordereaux).

docs.text:

  • Swiss Re — Proportional reinsurance fundamentals
  • Insurance textbooks on reinsurance structures (public domain)

docs.title: 15.4 — Excess of Loss & Stop Loss
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define non-proportional reinsurance and explain excess of loss (XL).
  2. Describe working layers, per-risk XL, and per-occurrence XL.
  3. Explain stop loss / aggregate protection.
  4. Calculate XL recoveries using attachment and limit.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Non-proportional reinsurance — principally excess of loss (XL) and stop loss — responds only when losses exceed a defined threshold. The reinsurer does not share every risk; it pays the amount of a loss above an attachment point, up to a limit. This structure protects the cedent against large individual losses (per risk XL), catastrophic events (cat XL), or poor aggregate experience (stop loss).

docs.title: 15.4.1 Non-Proportional Reinsurance
docs.text:
Unlike proportional reinsurance, non-proportional cover shares no part of premiums or losses by a fixed ratio. Instead:

Element Description Attachment (priority) Loss threshold before reinsurer pays Limit (capacity) Maximum reinsurer pays per loss/event Recovery Portion of loss between attachment and limit Premium Usually a percentage of the cedent's subject premium Reinstatement Cover may be reinstated after exhaustion, for additional premium

docs.title: Key Terminology
docs.text: Term Definition Burning cost Historic loss cost of the layer Rate on line Premium ÷ limit Risk premium Expected loss to the layer Exposure premium Premium based on portfolio characteristics Layer Band of protection (e.g., $5M xs $5M) Primary layer (working layer) Low attachment, high expected frequency Upper layers High attachment, low frequency

docs.title: 15.4.2 Per-Risk Excess of Loss
docs.text:
Per-risk XL protects the cedent against individual large losses on specific risks.

Element Description Basis Each risk / each loss separately Attachment Above cedent's retention per risk Limit Maximum recovery per risk Example $10M xs $5M — pays losses above $5M up to $15M

docs.title: Example Calculation
docs.text: Element Value Layer $10M xs $5M Loss $8M Cedent retention $5M Reinsurer recovery $3M Remaining layer $7M unused

docs.title: 15.4.3 Per-Occurrence & Catastrophe XL
docs.text:
Per-occurrence XL / CAT XL responds to the aggregate of all losses arising from a single event.

Element Description Event definition Cause(s) of loss — windstorm, earthquake, flood Hours clause Time window defining one occurrence Area clause Geographic scope of an event Aggregate limit Max recovery for the event, often with reinstatements

docs.title: Catastrophe XL Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Single Event] --> B[All policy losses]
    B --> C{Above Retention?}
    C -->|No| D[Cedent retains all]
    C -->|Yes| E[Reinsurer pays up to limit]
    E --> F{Layer exhausted?}
    F -->|Reinstatement available| G[Cover restored]

docs.title: Example — CAT XL
docs.text: Element Value Layer $100M xs $50M (1 reinstatement) Event losses $250M Cedent retention $50M Reinsurer initial payment $100M (limit exhausted) Reinstatement Cover restored; second event up to $100M Reinstatement premium 100% of layer premium

docs.title: 15.4.4 Stop Loss (Aggregate Excess)
docs.text:
Stop loss protects the cedent's aggregate loss ratio on a portfolio.

Element Description Attachment Loss ratio threshold (e.g., 70%) Limit Max percentage / amount of recovery Basis Portfolio premium or incurred losses Purpose Protect against frequency deterioration

docs.title: Stop Loss Example
docs.text: Element Value Ceded premium $100,000,000 Loss ratio attachment 75% Stop loss limit 40 points (75% to 115%) Actual loss ratio 95% Recovery (95% − 75%) = 20 points × premium = $20M

docs.title: 15.4.5 XL vs Proportional Summary
docs.text: Aspect Proportional (QS/Surplus) Non-Proportional (XL) Premium Shared in cession ratio Premium paid for layer Losses Shared in cession ratio Paid above attachment Small losses Shared Not covered (retained) Large losses Shared Covered up to limit Administration Bordereaux, cessions Layer reporting, aggregations Pricing Commission-based Burning cost / exposure

docs.title: Burning Cost Approach
docs.text: Step Calculation 1 Collect historic losses 2 Trend to future values 3 Apply to current exposure 4 Reinsure to the layer 5 Derive burning cost = Expected losses ÷ Limit 6 Add loadings (expense, capital, profit)

docs.title: Pricing Components
docs.text: Component Description Burning cost Expected loss to layer Risk load Uncertainty / volatility Expense load Brokerage, administration Capital charge Return on capital Total premium Sum of components Rate on line Premium as % of limit

docs.title: 15.4.7 Reinstatements
docs.text: Element Description Purpose Restore the layer after exhaustion Premium % of original layer premium Free reinstatement No additional premium (rare) Paid reinstatement Standard — e.g., 100% or 50% Number Stated in the treaty (e.g., 1, 2, or unlimited)

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. What does "$10M xs $5M" mean and how is a recovery calculated?
  2. Distinguish per-risk XL from per-occurrence (CAT) XL.
  3. What is an hours clause in a CAT treaty?
  4. How does stop loss protect a portfolio?
  5. What is burning cost and how is it used in XL pricing?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Attachment Loss threshold for reinsurer payment Burning cost Historic expected loss to a layer Hours clause Time window defining one occurrence Reinstatement Restoration of cover after exhaustion Rate on line Premium ÷ limit

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. XL covers only losses above an attachment, up to a limit.
  2. Per-risk XL handles individual large losses; CAT XL handles event accumulations.
  3. Stop loss protects the aggregate loss ratio.
  4. XL pricing relies on expected loss (burning cost) plus loadings.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text:
• Swiss Re — Excess of loss reinsurance fundamentals
  • Reinsurance Association of America — non-proportional structures
  • Industry catastrophe model documentation

docs.title: 15.5 — Catastrophe Reinsurance & Retrocession
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain catastrophe risk and why catastrophe reinsurance is needed.
  2. Describe CAT XL structures, event definitions, and reinstatements.
  3. Explain catastrophe modelling and PML concepts.
  4. Define retrocession and alternative capital (ILS, cat bonds).

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Catastrophe reinsurance protects insurers against the financial impact of large natural events — windstorms, earthquakes, floods — that create massive accumulations of loss across a portfolio. CAT XL layers respond per single event and often include reinstatements. Insurers use catastrophe models to quantify probable maximum loss (PML), then transfer the tail risk to reinsurers, retrocessionaires, and capital markets via insurance-linked securities (ILS) such as catastrophe bonds.

docs.title: 15.5.1 What Is Catastrophe Risk?
docs.text:
Catastrophe (CAT) risk is the potential for a single event — or a season of events — to produce losses across many policies simultaneously.

Element Description Peril Windstorm, earthquake, flood, wildfire, freeze, terrorism Event Defined by cause, time (hours clause), and area Accumulation Sum of insured exposures in the event zone Correlation Many policies impacted by one event Severity Potential losses far exceed normal frequency

docs.title: Major Catastrophe Types
docs.text: Peril Characteristics Modelling Windstorm Wind speed, tracks Rerun thousands of simulated events Earthquake Ground motion, soil Fault lines, shaking intensity Flood River, coastal, flash Hydrological models Wildfire Fuel, wind, interface Fire spread simulation Severe storm Hail, tornado, straight-line Convective storm models Winter storm Snow, ice Meteorological models

docs.title: 15.5.2 Catastrophe XL Structures
docs.text: Element Description Layer E.g., $250M xs $100M Event One catastrophe occurrence per treaty definition Hours clause E.g., 72 hours continuous for windstorm Area clause E.g., losses within defined region Limit Max recovery per event Reinstatements Usually 1–2, with additional premium Annual aggregate Optional cap on total recoveries

docs.title: Tower of Protection
docs.text: Layer Limit Attachment Purpose Working XL $10M $5M Frequent moderate losses Middle layer $50M $100M Severe events Catastrophe layer $250M $150M Top catastrophic risk Retrocession / ILS $300M $400M Tail / capital market

docs.title: Model Components
docs.text: Component Function Hazard Intensity of event at each location Exposure Insured values, construction, occupancy Vulnerability Damage as a function of intensity Financial Policy conditions, deductibles, limits, reinsurance

docs.title: Model Outputs
docs.text: Metric Definition PML (Probable Maximum Loss) Loss at a selected return period OEP (Occurrence Exceedance Probability) Probability of loss from one event AEP (Aggregate Exceedance Probability) Probability of annual aggregate loss AAL (Average Annual Loss) Expected loss per year Return period 1 in 100, 1 in 250 for PML

docs.title: PML Illustration
docs.text: Return Period PML (OEP) 1 in 50 $80M 1 in 100 $120M 1 in 250 $180M 1 in 500 $250M

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Description Expected loss (AAL to layer) Modelled loss cost Risk load Volatility and uncertainty Capital charge Return on collateral/capital Expense & commission Costs of placement Technical premium Sum of the above Market adjustment Supply/demand, market hardening/softening

docs.title: Rate on Line
docs.text: Layer Limit Premium ROL CAT XL $250M xs $150M $50M 20%

docs.title: 15.5.5 Retrocession
docs.text:
Retrocession is reinsurance purchased by a reinsurer to protect its own portfolio.

Element Description Retrocedent The reinsurer ceding risk Retrocessionaire The reinsurer assuming the risk Purpose Reduce net exposure, peak peril risk, capital relief Forms Proportional or non-proportional retro treaties Linked Risk follows the original business

docs.title: Retrocession Example
docs.text: Entity Role Primary insurer Cedes to reinsurer Reinsurer Accepts; then cedes a layer to retrocessionaire Retrocessionaire Assumes share of the reinsurer's risk

docs.title: 15.5.6 Alternative Capital & ILS
docs.text: Instrument Description Catastrophe bond (cat bond) Investor principal at risk if trigger level breached Industry loss warranty (ILW) Payment based on industry loss index Sidecar Reinsurance vehicle sharing a book of business Collateralised reinsurance Funds held to secure obligations Swap / derivative Transfer catastrophe risk to capital markets

docs.title: Cat Bond Trigger Types
docs.text: Trigger Description Indemnity Based on cedent's actual losses Index Based on modelled or industry index Parametric Based on physical parameter (e.g., wind speed)

docs.title: 15.5.7 Case Study — Large Hurricane
docs.text:
Scenario: An insurer writes 1% of coastal wind exposure with $300M PML at 1-in-100.

Programme: - Retention: $50M - Working XL: $25M xs $25M - CAT layer: $200M xs $50M - Cat bond: $50M xs $250M

Outcome: A 1-in-100 event produces $120M of losses. The insurer retains $50M, recovers $25M from working XL and $45M from CAT layer, leaving large losses within its risk tolerance. The tail is protected by the cat bond.

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. What makes a loss "catastrophic" from a reinsurer's perspective?
  2. Define PML, OEP, AEP, and AAL.
  3. What is an hours clause and why is it used?
  4. Explain the difference between retrocession and reinsurance.
  5. How does a catastrophe bond differ from a traditional CAT XL?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition AAL Average annual loss AEP Aggregate exceedance probability Cat bond Capital-market catastrophe protection OEP Occurrence exceedance probability PML Probable maximum loss Retrocession Reinsurance of a reinsurer

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. CAT risk arises from correlated losses across many policies in one event.
  2. CAT XL provides per-event recoveries with reinstatements.
  3. Catastrophe models estimate PML and drive pricing and retention decisions.
  4. Retrocession and ILS shift the tail risk beyond the traditional reinsurance market.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text:
• AIR, RMS (Moody's), Verisk cat model documentation (public summaries)
  • Swiss Re Institute — sigma catastrophe reports
  • Insurance Information Institute — catastrophe fundamentals

docs.title: 15.6 — Reinsurance Pricing & Accounting
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the components of reinsurance premium pricing.
  2. Describe experience vs exposure rating methods.
  3. Explain key reinsurance accounting entries.
  4. Describe reporting, reserves, and regulatory treatment.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Reinsurance pricing combines the expected loss cost of the coverage (burning cost) with loadings for expenses, capital, and profit. Methods include experience rating (based on the cedent's own loss history) and exposure rating (based on portfolio characteristics). Accounting for reinsurance involves ceded premium, ceding commission, recoveries, and reserves, with treatment governed by solvency frameworks (Solvency II, NAIC, IRDAI).

docs.title: Experience Rating
docs.text: Element Description Basis Cedent's historical losses Process Trend, develop, apply to current exposure Strengths Reflects actual portfolio Limitations Sparse data for large layers

docs.title: Exposure Rating
docs.text: Element Description Basis Estimated loss cost from exposure profiles Process Apply severity distributions to exposure Strengths Works for new/low-frequency layers Limitations Relies on modelled assumptions

docs.title: Burning Cost Derivation
docs.text: Step Description 1 Extract historic losses subject to the layer 2 Trend losses to future cost levels 3 Develop for IBNR / late reporting 4 Convert to current exposure base 5 Calculate annual expected loss to layer 6 Divide by limit to obtain burning cost

docs.title: 15.6.2 Pricing Components
docs.text: Component Description Example Burning cost Expected loss to layer $2.0M Risk load Uncertainty of loss $0.5M Capital charge Return on capital supporting the layer $0.8M Expense load Underwriting, administration, brokerage $0.6M Profit margin Target return $0.3M Technical premium Total $4.2M

docs.title: Price Monitoring Metrics
docs.text: Metric Formula Purpose Rate on line Premium ÷ Limit Price relative to exposure Loss ratio Loss ÷ Premium Claims experience Combined ratio (Loss + Expense) ÷ Premium Underwriting profitability Return on equity Profit ÷ Capital Capital efficiency

docs.title: 15.6.3 Accounting — Key Concepts
docs.text: Concept Description Ceded premium Premium transferred to reinsurer Ceding commission Reinsurer's payment to cedent for acquisition cost Profit commission Additional payment when treaty profitable Deposit premium Minimum premium at inception; adjusted later Provisional premium Estimate subject to adjustment Adjustment premium Difference between final and provisional Recoveries Reinsurer's share of paid losses Outstanding losses Reinsurer's share of reserves

docs.title: 15.6.4 Accounting Entries — Illustrative
docs.text: Transaction Cedent Debit Cedent Credit Pay ceded premium Ceded premium expense Cash / reinsurer Receive ceding commission Cash Ceding commission income Receive profit commission Cash Profit commission income Recover paid losses Cash / recoverable Recovered losses Record outstanding recoverable Recoverable asset Reserve offset

docs.title: 15.6.5 Reserves & Reporting
docs.text: Reserve Description Unearned premium reserve (UPR) Premium for unexpired risk Outstanding claims reserve (OCR) Reported losses unpaid IBNR Incurred but not reported losses Reserve for unexpired risk (RUR) Additional buffer when UPR insufficient

docs.title: Reporting Cycles
docs.text: Report Content Frequency Premium bordereau Ceded risks, premiums Monthly Loss bordereau Claims, recoveries Monthly Technical account Premium, claims, commissions Quarterly Annual statement Full-year account, settlement Annual

docs.title: 15.6.6 Regulatory Treatment
docs.text: Framework Treatment Solvency II (UK/EU) Credit for reinsurance if collateral/security requirements satisfied NAIC (US) Credit for reinsurance from authorised reinsurers; trust/collateral for others IRDAI (India) Reinsurance program approval; ceding limits Statutory reporting Reinsurer schedule in annual statement

docs.title: Key Regulatory Considerations
docs.text: Consideration Description Authorised vs unauthorised Credit allowed only for authorised (or collateralised) reinsurers Security & collateral Trust funds, letters of credit Retention & cession limits Minimum retention requirements Disclosure Reinsurance arrangements in regulatory filings

docs.title: 15.6.7 Case Study — Treaty Pricing
docs.text:
Scenario: Portfolio premium $100M; historical losses to a $20M xs $10M layer trended to $1.8M per year.

Calculation: - Burning cost = $1.8M - Risk load + capital + expense + profit = $1.4M - Technical premium = $3.2M (ROL = 16% of limit)

Outcome: If market ROL is 14%, the treaty is attractively priced; if 20%, the layer may be renegotiated or reduced.

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. Distinguish experience rating from exposure rating.
  2. List the components of a technical reinsurance premium.
  3. What is a ceding commission and why is it paid?
  4. Why does collateral matter for reinsurance credit?
  5. What is the difference between UPR and IBNR?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Burning cost Expected loss cost of a layer Ceding commission Reinsurer payment to cedent IBNR Incurred but not reported Rate on line Premium ÷ limit UPR Unearned premium reserve

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Experience and exposure methods estimate the expected loss cost.
  2. Technical premium = loss cost + risk + capital + expense + profit.
  3. Accounting tracks premium, commissions, recoveries, and reserves.
  4. Regulatory credit for reinsurance requires security and compliance.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text:
• Solvency II Directive — reinsurance provisions (public)
  • NAIC — reinsurance credit model law (public materials)
  • IRDAI — reinsurance regulations (public)

docs.title: 15.7 — Reinsurance Claims & Case Studies
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe the reinsurance claims notification and recovery process.
  2. Explain follow-the-fortunes and claims cooperation.
  3. Calculate reinsurance recoveries for proportional and XL treaties.
  4. Apply learning through worked case studies.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Reinsurance claims begin when the ceding company notifies the reinsurer of a loss that may attach to the treaty. Recoveries are calculated under the treaty terms — proportionally for quota share/surplus-based on the ceded share, or by layer for excess of loss. Key principles include follow-the-fortunes, claims cooperation, and timely notification.

docs.title: 15.7.1 Claims Notification
docs.text: Stage Action 1 Cedent identifies potential reinsurance involvement 2 Notify reinsurer per treaty notice terms 3 Provide claim details, loss advice, initial reserve 4 Reinsurer acknowledges, requests information 5 Ongoing updates per reporting schedule

docs.title: Notification Requirements
docs.text: Item Typical Requirement Timeliness As soon as loss known Threshold Loss above stated amount Frequency Initial, quarterly, on material change Content Policy, cause, amounts, reserves

docs.title: Proportional Treaty
docs.text: Element Value Claim $200,000 Ceded share 40% Recovery $80,000

docs.title: Excess of Loss
docs.text: Element Value Layer $10M xs $5M Claim $8M Cedent retention $5M Recovery $3M

docs.title: 15.7.3 Key Clauses
docs.text: Clause Description Follow the fortunes Reinsurer follows cedent's claims decisions made in good faith Follow the settlements Reinsurer follows cedent's settlements within terms Claims cooperation Both parties cooperate on significant claims Ultimate net loss (UNL) Loss after deductibles and other recoveries Loss adjustment expense (LAE) Costs of settling claims, often included in UNL

docs.title: 15.7.4 Reinsurance Claims Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Underlying claim] --> B{Cedent notifies reinsurer}
    B --> C[Reinsurer acknowledges]
    C --> D{Attaches to treaty?}
    D -->|No| E[No recovery]
    D -->|Yes| F[Calculate share / layer]
    F --> G[Recovery claim submitted]
    G --> H[Reinsurer pays / disputes]
    H --> I[Recovery recorded]
    I --> J[Case closed]

docs.title: 15.7.5 Common Disputes
docs.text: Dispute Description Mitigation Coverage wording Ambiguity on inclusion Clear treaty drafting Aggregation Event definition disagreement Hours/area clauses Notice failure Late notification Confirm notice terms Reserving difference Reserve adequacy Consistent valuation methods Allocation Multi-year/multi-risk claims Allocation provisions

docs.title: Case Study 1 — Proportional Recovery
docs.text:
Scenario: Quota share treaty 50%. Property claim of $1.2M.

Recovery: $600,000. Cedent retains $600,000. Both share premium and losses equally.

docs.title: Case Study 2 — XL Recovery
docs.text:
Scenario: $25M xs $10M per risk XL. Three claims: $8M, $12M, $6M.

  • Claim 1: $8M — below attachment, no recovery
  • Claim 2: $12M — recovery $2M
  • Claim 3: $6M — below attachment, no recovery
  • Total recoveries: $2M

docs.title: Case Study 3 — Catastrophe Event
docs.text:
Scenario: CAT XL $100M xs $50M, 1 reinstatement at 100%. Windstorm generates $180M portfolio loss.

  • Retention: $50M
  • Initial recovery: $100M (layer exhausted)
  • Reinstatement premium: 100% of layer premium paid
  • Second event: another $60M → recovery $60M

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the steps in notifying a reinsurer of a claim.
  2. What is the difference between follow-the-fortunes and follow-the-settlements?
  3. Calculate the recovery on a $15M claim under a $10M xs $5M layer.
  4. Why are hours/area clauses important in catastrophe claims?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Follow the fortunes Reinsurer adopts cedent's claims decisions LAE Loss adjustment expense UNL Ultimate net loss Recovery Amount paid by reinsurer

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Reinsurance claims require timely notification and documentation.
  2. Recoveries follow treaty structure — proportional share or XL layer.
  3. Follow-the-fortunes and cooperation clauses govern cedent/reinsurer relations.
  4. Case studies illustrate the practical application of treaties.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text:
• Reinsurance Association of America — claims best practices
  • Lloyd's claims framework materials

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Insurance fraud is a deliberate deception to obtain a benefit under an insurance policy or to avoid a premium obligation. It affects every line of business and adds billions to premium costs worldwide.

docs.title: 17.1.1 Key Concepts

docs.title: Fraud Types

docs.title: Where Fraud Occurs
docs.text: Indicator Description Action Application Misstatement at quote Medical history, garaging Claims Fabrication, inflation Most fraud is in claims Premium Misclassification Payroll, employee count Distribution Agent/broker schemes Premium diversion

docs.title: 17.1.3 Prevention & Response
docs.text: Stage Action Prevention Application screening, verification Detection Claims triage, analytics, referral rules Investigation SIU analysis, evidence collection Resolution Decline, rescission, referral to authorities

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text: 1. Distinguish hard fraud from soft fraud.\n2. Why is soft fraud more common?\n3. What are the costs of fraud to insurers?

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Hard fraud Fabricated loss

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text: 1. Fraud is deliberate deception for financial gain.\n2. Most fraud is soft fraud — exaggeration and misstatement.\n3. Fraud raises premiums and requires prevention investment.

docs.text:
